title: The hypertrophy series: why using metabolic stress for muscle growth fails
summary: NH argues that the pump comes from fast reps with light weight rather than from muscle damage. Training for it leads to mechanical failure (acid, blood) instead of muscular failure, which makes it junk volume. Most growth comes from heavy, intense sets taken to muscular failure, and a set that can be repeated almost identically a minute later was not damaging.
claims: Much of the pump chasing came from pro bodybuilders on PEDs
The pump comes from rapid lengthening and contraction of muscle fibres at a high tempo with light weight, not from how much damage is done; fast empty-bar curls pump more than heavy curls
Squatting about 20% of your back squat for max reps gives a huge quad pump but is not a good way to grow, because it ignores intensity windows
People who only do light weight for reps see temporary pump results but no long-term progress, because growth comes from strength progression over time increasing tonnage
NH is not anti-pump; increased blood flow may have some hypertrophy benefits, but most hypertrophy comes from muscle fibre damage done with heavy weight
Use multiple rep ranges, higher reps and lower reps, and even high-rep sets must go to failure within relevant intensity windows
Muscular failure differs from mechanical failure: with an empty bar a rep calculator might predict 122 curls but you stop at 48 because blood and acid shut you down, not the muscle
Bodybuilders should avoid being stopped by the pump; the fix is high-intensity windows, where heavy sets are rarely ended by pump and still grow you more
Blood flow restriction and pump-focused drop sets are junk volume, because a weight light enough to let the pump stop you is not challenging enough
If you can move a weight fast enough to pump just from speed, it is not challenging; very high rep targets push people to rush early reps
A truly intense top set cannot be repeated 20 seconds later, or even the same day; after a true max set of two, 10-15 minutes of rest should not be enough to hit it again
If you can rest a minute and nearly match a set, or do 55 push-ups then 53 two minutes later, the exercise is not damaging and not driving growth
The main drivers of hypertrophy are volume, intensity and frequency; metabolic stress is an accessory at best
exercises: demonstration that the pump comes from tempo, not damage
advanced lifters' high-rep sets show little damage when repeatable
